questions.prompt: Robust performance, for a set of plants around a nominal model, means
questions.explanation: Nominal stability and a single-frequency reading of \(|T|\) can both hold while a plant inside the uncertainty set misses the spec. Robust performance is the spec on that whole set. Zero weights would make the spec empty, which is not a performance requirement.

questions.prompt: At one frequency, \(|W_s S| = 0.40\) and \(|W_m T| = 0.35\). The robust-performance quantity \(|W_s S| + |W_m T|\) is
questions.explanation: The two nonnegative terms add: \(0.40 + 0.35 = 0.75\). Their product \(0.14\) is not the test. The larger term alone, \(0.40\), is a piece of the sum, and passing each piece is a weaker statement than passing the sum. The difference \(0.05\) has no role in the test.

questions.prompt: On the nominal plant, \(|S| = 0.5\) and the performance weight is \(|W_s| = 1.2\). The nominal-performance quantity \(|W_s S|\) is
questions.explanation: Nominal performance at this frequency is the product \(1.2 \times 0.5 = 0.6\). The sum \(1.7\) adds a weight to a sensitivity as if they were the same kind of number. The ratio \(1.2 / 0.5 = 2.4\) inverts the sensitivity. Reporting \(0.5\) drops the weight that defines the spec.

questions.prompt: At one frequency the magnitudes are ws, sm, wm, and tm, in that order: performance weight, sensitivity, multiplicative weight, complementary sensitivity. Write \(|W_s S| + |W_m T|\) in the names ws, sm, wm, and tm.
questions.explanation: Each weight multiplies its own sensitivity. The robust-performance quantity is \(w_s s_m + w_m t_m\). The product of all four is a different expression. Adding the weights to the sensitivities, instead of multiplying, mixes units the test does not add. Swapping partners, \(w_s t_m + w_m s_m\), puts each weight on the wrong function.

questions.prompt: At the frequency you are checking, \(|W_s| = 0.5\), \(|S| = 0.9\), \(|W_m| = 0.4\), and \(|T| = 1.1\). The quantity \(|W_s S| + |W_m T|\) is
questions.explanation: \(0.5 \times 0.9 = 0.45\) and \(0.4 \times 1.1 = 0.44\). The sum is 0.89. Adding the four numbers, \(2.9\), treats weights and sensitivities as terms rather than factors. The larger product alone, \(0.45\), drops the uncertainty term. Because \(0.89 < 1\), this one frequency passes; the infinity-norm test still has to hold at every frequency.

questions.prompt: Put these checks in the order you would run them for multiplicative uncertainty.
questions.explanation: An unstable nominal loop makes the later peaks meaningless, so stability is first. Nominal performance and robust stability are the two separate bills. The sum is a stricter bill than either one, so it comes after you know which of the pieces already failed. Raising the gain everywhere is the last resort, and it is often the wrong one, because it shrinks \(S\) and grows \(T\).

steps: Confirm the nominal loop is stable.
Check nominal performance, the peak of |W_s S| below 1.
Check robust stability, the peak of |W_m T| below 1.
Check robust performance: the peak, over frequency, of the sum |W_s S| + |W_m T| is below 1.
If the sum fails, loosen the performance weight or shrink the uncertainty before raising the loop gain at every frequency.

questions.prompt: Multiplicative uncertainty, and a performance weight on \(S\). One step is wrong.
questions.explanation: Both readings are taken at \(4\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), so the robust-performance quantity there is \(0.7 + 0.5 = 1.2\). That is not a sum of peaks from two different frequencies. Each piece below 1 does not put the sum below 1, so robust stability and nominal performance pass while robust performance fails. The first two readings are the right separate tests, and the last step is the repair.

steps: At \(4\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), \(|W_m T| = 0.7\), and that is its largest value, so robust stability passes.
At that same frequency, \(|W_s S| = 0.5\), and that is its largest value, so nominal performance passes.
Their sum at \(4\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) is \(1.2\), but robust performance still passes because each piece passed on its own.
Robust performance uses \(|W_s S| + |W_m T|\) at each frequency, so \(1.2\) at this frequency fails the test.
reasons: At one frequency, each piece below 1 does not make |W_s S| + |W_m T| below 1.
A robust-stability pass cancels the performance weight.
Nominal performance is checked on T, not on S.

questions.explanation: \(S + T = 1\) means the two complex values add to 1. They cannot both have small magnitude at the same frequency, so a weight on \(S\) and a weight on \(T\) at that frequency are asking for two things the identity will not give. The sum of the magnitudes is not identically 1. A high gain drives \(S\) toward 0 and \(T\) toward 1, not both toward 0.

questions.prompt: Which statements hold for the multiplicative robust-performance test?
questions.explanation: The sum of two nonnegative functions is at least as large as either one, so a sum below 1 forces each piece below 1, while either piece can sit below 1 with the sum above 1. Raising the loop gain shrinks \(S\) and pushes \(T\) toward 1, so it does not shrink both.

options: Nominal performance can pass while robust performance fails.
Robust stability can pass while robust performance fails.
If the peak of \(|W_s S| + |W_m T|\) is below 1, then the peaks of \(|W_s S|\) and of \(|W_m T|\) are also below 1.
Raising the loop gain at every frequency makes both \(S\) and \(T\) smaller.

questions.prompt: At the frequency where \(|W_s S| + |W_m T|\) is largest, the two terms are \(0.55\) and \(0.30\). How far below 1 is that sum?
questions.explanation: The sum is \(0.85\), and the room under the bound is \(1 - 0.85 = 0.15\). Reporting \(0.85\) returns the sum rather than the gap. Reporting \(0.55\) returns one term. Reporting \(0.45\), which is \(1 - 0.55\), is the room under the larger term alone and ignores the \(0.30\) that is also in the sum.

questions.prompt: The combined bound fails only near the gain crossover. The useful next move is to
questions.explanation: Near crossover, \(|S|\) and \(|T|\) are both order one, so the two weights are active together. Moving the crossover, or shaping the slope there, is how you separate them. A right-half-plane cancellation would hide an unstable mode. A failed sum is not a proof that the nominal loop is unstable. Dropping \(S\) drops the performance spec the test was written to protect.

questions.prompt: The uncertainty is a slow drift of one parameter, not a fixed set you must cover with one controller. Compared with enlarging \(W_m\) until the combined test barely passes,
questions.explanation: A fixed controller that works for every value in a wide set has to satisfy the sum bound for the whole set, which shrinks the performance you can ask for. If the parameter actually drifts and can be estimated while the loop runs, updating the controller from that estimate is a different design, and it is not the same as inflating \(W_m\). A larger weight makes the test harder. The spec does not forbid feedback.
